title: Timing run: how long does a person actually wait, generated SQL vs today's Python?
spec:
THE SECOND RUN Evan funded (his Q6). Full spec: spikes/T-1/EXPERIMENTS.md section 2.

EVAN RE-SPECIFIED THIS RUN'S BAR HIMSELF, verbatim: 'Benchmark absolute user-facing latency rather than treating a 3.79x-7.15x relative slowdown as intrinsically fatal.' A 3.79x slowdown on an 8 ms query is 30 ms and nobody notices; the same ratio at a million rows is seconds. So the bar is milliseconds waited, not a ratio.

QUESTION: at realistic row counts, how long does a person wait for the generated SQL compared with GIMS's current in-memory path?

BLOCKED ON EVAN — the bar is a number only he can set. EXPERIMENTS.md section 2.2 offers three, each grounded in a measurement: 2,500 ms at one million rows (proposed), 5,500 ms (the earlier panel's floor converted to milliseconds), or 8,331 ms (marked as a kill line rather than a bar). He picks or names his own.

BINDING CONSTRAINTS:
- Q11: no database indexes. The measured 3.79x-7.15x gap is therefore a floor, not a starting point — index use was the only route by which it could have closed.
- Q8 / follow-up item 7: no real widget was named, so the run uses an invented subset-legal widget, LABELLED as invented in the readout. If Evan names a real one before the run starts it substitutes directly and nothing else changes.
- The scratch database is gone (follow-up item 31: 'Leave it gone'), so the 1k-to-1M corpus must be rebuilt from proto/load_data.py first. Written instructions for that are still outstanding — his Q31 note.
- Needs an exclusive quiet window on the host; a loaded machine makes the result inadmissible.
